title: The Philippians 2 Hymn

keyTerms.d: If Paul is quoting an existing piece — a hymn, a confession, a creedal fragment — then its theology is older than the letter that contains it. That Paul is quoting is the majority view, though the pre-Pauline origin is itself debated: Gordon Fee argues Paul composed the hymn, and some have questioned whether “hymn” is the right genre label.

The word morphē does not mean mere outward shape, as if Christ only looked divine. A few words later the same noun describes what Christ became — the “form of a servant” (v. 7) — and by the logic of the parallel, the “form of God” he started in must be equally real.

The rare noun behind “a thing to be grasped” (v. 6), among the most contested words in the New Testament. On one reading equality with God is a thing not yet possessed that Christ refused to seize; on the other, a thing already possessed that he refused to exploit. The word remains the subject of live philological dispute.

It does not say Christ emptied himself of anything — the Greek has no genitive “of his deity.” Grammatically, the sentence tells us how he emptied himself: “by taking the form of a servant.” The mystery is not subtraction but addition and concealment; he did not set aside, lose, or diminish his deity.

In its original context one of the most fiercely monotheistic passages in all of Scripture: YHWH declares “I am God, and there is no other” and swears that to him alone “every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.” The hymn takes that text and applies it to Jesus.

Almost certainly the divine name itself, rendered Kyrios (“Lord”) — the Greek Old Testament’s standard substitute for YHWH. The confession “Jesus Christ is Lord” thus places Jesus on the divine side of the line that Jewish monotheism drew most sharply.

Bauckham’s reading: Second Temple Jews defined the one God by who he is — the sole Creator, the sole sovereign, the only one worthy of worship — and the hymn includes Jesus within that unique identity. Widely influential, though the category itself is debated (James F. McGrath disputes it).

Dunn’s rival reading: Adam grasped at equality with God and was condemned; Christ, the second Adam, faced the same archetypal choice, refused to grasp, and was exalted. On this reading every line maps onto a contrast between two men, and the hymn need not assert that Christ personally existed before Bethlehem at all. Wright grants the genuine Adam echoes but argues they are woven into a frame the Adam reading cannot carry: the sequence “in the form of God… taking the form of a servant” describes a transition Adam never made.

derive.q: The passage is balanced, rhythmic, almost liturgical, and many judge that Paul is quoting rather than composing — so its theology is…?
derive.ans: older than the letter (only as secure as the pre-Pauline premise)
derive.why: Philippians was written in the mid-50s or early 60s; if Paul is indeed quoting prior material, that material predates the letter — plausibly reaching back into the 40s, within a couple of decades of the crucifixion. The inference is only as secure as the pre-Pauline premise itself, which some scholars question.

derive.q: The same noun, morphē, names both the “form of God” Christ was in and the “form of a servant” he took — so the “form of God” is…?
derive.why: His servanthood was not a costume; he genuinely became a servant. By the logic of the parallel, the “form of God” he started in must be equally real. The phrase points to Christ’s sharing in the very condition and glory of God.

derive.q: “He emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” — and the Greek names nothing he emptied himself of. So the self-emptying is…?
derive.why: The Greek has no genitive “of his deity”: grammatically, the sentence tells us how he emptied himself — “by taking the form of a servant.” On the reading Gordon Fee defends, the self-emptying is the taking-on, not a laying-down. How exactly to understand the “emptying” has itself been debated, but he did not set aside, lose, or diminish his deity. As Gregory of Nazianzus put it: “What He was He continued to be; what He was not He took to Himself.”

derive.q: The climax lifts YHWH’s oath from Isaiah 45 — where he swears that to him alone every knee shall bow — and centres it on Jesus. So Jesus is placed…?
derive.ans: on the divine side of the line
derive.why: It is a text about the worship owed to the one God of Israel and to no one else, and the hymn applies it to Jesus. The “name above every name” he is given is almost certainly the divine name itself, rendered Kyrios — so the confession places Jesus on the divine side of the line that Jewish monotheism drew most sharply.

derive.q: “Form of God” and “equality with God” both stand in verse 6, before the “therefore” of verse 9 — so the exaltation…?
derive.ans: vindicates a status already possessed (on the Hoover–Wright reading)
derive.why: On the Hoover–Wright reading defended above, that equality was already his; the “therefore” of verse 9 rewards the self-humbling of one who was already “in the form of God.” The exaltation restores and publicly vindicates a status already possessed, and confers a name — a public station — not a divine nature the exalted one had previously lacked.

derive.q: Grant all of it. Does the hymn, by itself, deliver the full doctrine of the Trinity or the two-natures formula of Chalcedon?
derive.ans: no — it is one strand, and a poetic one
derive.why: Those took centuries of reflection to articulate. The hymn is poetry, not the creed of Chalcedon, and it leaves much unspoken about how the divine and human are related. But it is an extraordinary strand: the worship of Jesus as God is found, already confessed, at the headwaters of the Christian movement.

honestState.p1: Several things are widely (not universally) agreed, and several remain contested. That Paul is quoting pre-existing material is the majority view, though the pre-Pauline origin is itself debated. The “exploited / used to advantage” reading of harpagmos is now common in major commentaries, but the word remains the subject of live philological dispute. And the pre-existence question — Dunn versus Wright, Fee, Bauckham, and Hurtado — is a real and ongoing scholarly debate, not a settled rout, though the weight of recent scholarship has moved toward reading genuine pre-existence in the text.
honestState.fairness: The rival reading should be stated at full strength: Dunn argues from the text that the hymn is Adam Christology, in which every line maps onto a contrast between two men and the hymn need not assert that Christ personally existed before Bethlehem at all; in his judgment the clearest statement of personal pre-existence in the New Testament is in John’s Gospel, and he nuanced his position in response to critics without abandoning the Adam reading. Gordon Fee argues Paul composed the hymn; Hurtado himself questioned whether “hymn” is the right genre label; and Bauckham’s divine-identity category is widely influential but debated — James F. McGrath disputes it.
honestState.verdict: The Carmen Christi does not, by itself, deliver the full doctrine of the Trinity or the two-natures formula of Chalcedon. But it shows that, if Paul is indeed quoting earlier material — the majority view — then within perhaps two decades of the crucifixion, Jewish followers of Jesus were confessing him as one who shared the “form of God,” who was given the divine name, and to whom they applied a text Isaiah had reserved for YHWH alone. Whatever the unresolved questions about a single Greek word, the worship of Jesus as God is not a late accretion. We hold that this worship is rightly placed — that the one they sang to is, as Nicaea confessed, true God from true God, fully God and fully man.

order: Philippians 2:6–11 preserves an early Christian hymn, older than the letter that quotes it.
The hymn says Christ existed in the form of God and applies YHWH’s Isaiah 45:23 oath to him.
Therefore the worship of Jesus as Lord is not a later legend.

props.t: being in the form of God, he took the form of a servant
emptied himself by taking the form of a servant
YHWH’s Isaiah 45:23 oath applied to Jesus
given the name above every name
confessed as Lord to the glory of God the Father
made equal with God only at the end of the story
the pre-existence reading is a settled rout
states the whole doctrine of Chalcedon by itself

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: Philippians 2:6–11 preserves an early Christian hymn, composed before the letter (mid-50s or early 60s), within perhaps two decades of the crucifixion. Limit: the dating is only as secure as the pre-Pauline premise itself — the majority view, but itself debated.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and what it does not say.
cards.a: The hymn says Christ existed in the form of God, emptied himself to take a servant’s form, and that every knee will bow and every tongue confess him as Lord, quoting Isaiah 45:23. It does not say he emptied himself of anything — the Greek has no genitive “of his deity.”

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the worship of Jesus as Lord is not a later legend: the argument’s force is chronological, removing the time legend needs. It does not, by itself, deliver the Trinity or Chalcedon; it is poetry, and leaves much unspoken about how the divine and human are related.

cards.q: Why can “form of God” not mean mere outward shape?
cards.a: Because the same noun describes what Christ became — the “form of a servant.” His servanthood was not a costume; by the logic of the parallel, the “form of God” he started in must be equally real.

cards.q: What does “emptied himself” mean — and not mean?
cards.a: The sentence tells how he emptied himself: “by taking the form of a servant.” The self-emptying is the taking-on, not a laying-down — addition and concealment, not subtraction. He remained what he was and took up what he was not; his deity was not set aside, lost, or diminished.

cards.q: Why does the Isaiah 45:23 citation carry so much weight?
cards.a: In Isaiah it is one of the most fiercely monotheistic passages in Scripture: YHWH declares there is no other and swears that to him alone every knee shall bow. A text about the worship owed to the one God and to no one else is applied to Jesus.

cards.q: What is “the name above every name,” and why does it matter?
cards.a: Almost certainly the divine name itself, rendered Kyrios — the Greek Old Testament’s standard substitute for YHWH. So the confession “Jesus Christ is Lord” places Jesus on the divine side of the line Jewish monotheism drew most sharply.

cards.q: How does the hymn itself rule out a second god?
cards.a: Its last line: the universal confession of Jesus as Lord does not rival the Father or divide the Godhead — it redounds to the Father’s glory (v. 11). That is why the earliest Jewish believers could bow to Jesus without supposing they had gained a second god.

cards.q: Reply to: the hymn contrasts two men, Adam and Christ.
cards.a: Paul genuinely uses Adam–Christ typology, one of his richest ways of asserting Christ’s true humanity. But Wright and Fee answer that a merely human second Adam was never “in the form of God” before “taking the form of a servant” and being “born in the likeness of men” — a transition Adam never made; Fee adds that the parallel morphē theou / morphē doulou resists being flattened into two human postures, and the morphē language and the Isaiah 45 climax resist a purely human Jesus. Still, the pre-existence question is a real and ongoing scholarly debate, not a settled rout.

cards.q: On harpagmos — what is the honest concession, and why does the case survive it?
cards.a: The word is contested and confident lexical certainty is impossible. But the reading that he refused to exploit an equality he already had does not depend on the word alone: it is reinforced by the morphē language and the Isaiah 45 climax, neither of which fits a purely human Jesus comfortably.

cards.q: Against the critic who grants pre-existence but calls the pre-existent one an angel — where does the dispute lie, and what decides it?
cards.a: The dispute is about kind, not date: what is denied of the pre-existent figure is not his early date but his rank. What decides it is the text the hymn quotes — Isaiah surrounds the oath with “there is no other,” so a creature lifted into that worship is precisely the “other” the oath excludes.

cards.q: If the hymn were set aside entirely, would pre-existence fall with it?
cards.a: Not on Fee’s reading: as Gordon Fee observed, Paul nowhere sets out to prove that Christ pre-existed; across more than a decade of letters he everywhere assumes it, as settled common ground. And the same descent surfaces in letters no one reads as a hymn: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), which reads most naturally — though a metaphor of earthly poverty is possible — as a transition from a prior state.

obj.q: Read it as Adam Christology. Adam, made in God’s image, grasped at equality with God and was condemned; Christ, the second Adam, refused to grasp, obeyed to death, and was exalted. Every line maps onto two men — the hymn need not say Christ existed before Bethlehem at all.
obj.model: This is the most serious challenge, and it argues from the text, so the answer must come from the text. Paul genuinely uses Adam–Christ typology, and it is one of his richest ways of asserting Christ’s true humanity. But the typology does not reduce Christ to a merely human second Adam. Wright grants the genuine Adam echoes but argues they are woven into a frame the Adam reading cannot carry: a merely human second Adam was never “in the form of God” before “taking the form of a servant” and being “born in the likeness of men.” That sequence — being in God’s form, then becoming human — describes a transition Adam never made. Fee adds that the parallel morphē theou / morphē doulou resists being flattened into two human postures. And no Adam typology explains giving Jesus YHWH’s own Isaiah 45 oath. Still, the pre-existence question is a real and ongoing scholarly debate, not a settled rout.

obj.q: The Greek says he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped — seized. You do not seize what you already own. The verse denies he had equality.
obj.model: The harpagmos debate is genuinely unsettled; the word is so rare that confident lexical certainty is impossible. A widely cited study by Roy W. Hoover examined the idiom across Greek literature and argued it consistently meant treating something already at one’s disposal as a prize to be used for one’s own advantage, and N. T. Wright built on it: the verse is not about Christ refusing to grab deity but about his refusing to exploit a divine equality he already had. The honest concession is that the word is contested; but that reading does not depend on it alone — it is reinforced by the morphē language and the Isaiah 45 climax, neither of which fits a purely human Jesus comfortably. So the verse cannot be made to deny that he had equality: the objection needs the other sense, an equality not yet possessed — the very sense in dispute — while on the Hoover–Wright reading that equality was already his, and the verse says he refused to exploit it.

obj.q: “Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name” — that is a reward. Even Bart Ehrman, who grants the hymn teaches pre-existence, reads the pre-existent one as an angel: equality with God is the prize at the end of the story, not its starting point.
obj.model: The dispute is about kind, not date: Ehrman grants pre-existence, and what he denies is rank. Everything he places at the end, the hymn names at the beginning: “in the form of God” and “equality with God” both stand in verse 6 — before the incarnation, before the cross, and before the “therefore” of verse 9. On the Hoover–Wright reading defended above, that equality was already his. The exaltation restores and publicly vindicates a status already possessed, and confers a name — a public station — not a divine nature the exalted one had previously lacked; and the one exalted is exalted as truly man, without ever ceasing to be what he was. The decisive difficulty is the text the hymn quotes: Isaiah surrounds those words with “I am God, and there is no other” (45:22), and elsewhere says “my glory I give to no other” (42:8). An angel lifted into that oath is precisely the “other” the oath excludes. Grant, for argument’s sake, that God’s name and authority could be entrusted to a supreme agent; the worship still could not be. And within the New Testament, faithful angels refuse worship (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9) — yet in the hymn the knees in heaven bow to Jesus. So the honest answer is no: the hymn does not fit an angel Christology.

obj.q: Scholars now dispute that it is a pre-Pauline hymn at all — maybe Paul wrote it himself. Then your early date collapses to the date of the letter.
obj.model: Take the worst case: Paul composed it for this letter, in the mid-50s or early 60s — still within three decades, and presented to a congregation as uncontroversial common ground. And the case never rested on the dating alone. As Gordon Fee observed, Paul nowhere sets out to prove that Christ pre-existed; across more than a decade of letters he everywhere assumes it, in the offhand way a writer treats settled common ground. An assumption that pervasive is harder to explain away than any explicit proof would be. The same descent surfaces in letters no one reads as a hymn: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9) reads most naturally — though a metaphor of earthly poverty is possible — as a transition from a prior state. So even if the Philippians hymn were set aside entirely, the pre-existence it sings would still stand in Paul.

unseen.q: Paul tells the Galatians they received him “as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus” (Galatians 4:14). Ehrman argues that when Paul uses that construction he is not contrasting two things but saying they are the same thing. By clear implication, Christ is an angel — and the hymn is the story of an angel who humbly became human.
unseen.model: That verse cannot bear the weight laid on it. The grammar allows that reading; it does not require it. Hurtado noted that even Charles Gieschen, whose work Ehrman follows here, offers it only as a “possibility,” and that most scholars read the verse as “a kind of stair-step statement,” with “angel of God” and “Christ Jesus” as ascending categories: you welcomed me as you would an angel — indeed, as you would Christ himself. The verse implies only that Paul was welcomed with an honour fit for an angel — indeed for Christ himself — not that Christ is an angel. Paul’s plain statements, meanwhile, put Christ on the other side of the line. Angels appear among the powers that cannot “separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39); believers will “judge angels” (1 Corinthians 6:3); and Christ is the “one Lord” “through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6) — and the one by whom every created thing was made cannot himself be one of the created things. One disputed verse, read against its most natural sense, cannot outweigh all of that.
unseen.source: library/phil2.html — “Bart Ehrman and the angel who was promoted,” Galatians 4:14 paragraph (Ehrman, How Jesus Became God, ch. 7, fn 18; Hurtado and Schenck, fn 24)
